nameStory: The whooper swan gets its name from its incredibly loud, trumpet-like call that sounds like "whoop-whoop-whoop" and can be heard from miles away. This powerful voice earned it the "whooper" nickname, distinguishing it from the quieter mute swan. In some places, it's also called the "common swan," though there's nothing common about spotting one in New England!
description: The whooper swan is a magnificent, pure white waterbird and one of the largest swans in the world. These impressive birds have long, graceful necks, powerful wings, and bright yellow bills with black tips. They're massive birds, comparable in size to trumpeter swans, with wingspans that can stretch over 8 feet across. Originally from Europe and Asia, whooper swans are extremely rare visitors to New England waters.

idTips.label: Bill Pattern
idTips.description: Bright yellow bill with a black tip, where the yellow extends past the nostrils in a distinctive wedge shape - this is the key field mark that separates it from other swans

idTips.label: Neck Posture
idTips.description: Holds its long neck perfectly straight and upright, like a white exclamation point on the water, rather than curved in an S-shape

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Incredibly loud, bugling "whoop-whoop-whoop" calls that sound like a trumpet and carry for miles - much more vocal than mute swans

idTips.label: Overall Size
idTips.description: Massive and imposing on the water, noticeably larger than most waterfowl with a heavy, powerful build and broad wingspan

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Clean white head with no black facial markings, appearing smooth and rounded without the prominent forehead knob of mute swans

habitat: In New England, whooper swans would most likely appear on large, open bodies of water like coastal bays, large lakes, or major river systems. They prefer areas with shallow water where they can reach aquatic plants by "tipping up" like giant ducks. Any sighting would likely be during migration periods near major flyways or coastal areas.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring vagrant that might appear during March-May migration periods. Would likely be spotted with other waterfowl during peak migration.
seasonality.summer: Not expected during summer months as they don't breed in North America. Any summer sighting would be extraordinary and worth reporting to birding authorities.
seasonality.fall: Most likely season for a vagrant sighting during October-December when they're migrating. Would probably appear as a single bird mixed in with other swans or waterfowl.
seasonality.winter: Possible but very rare winter visitor, especially along the coast where waters remain unfrozen. Would need open water and aquatic vegetation to survive.

funFact: Whooper swans are so incredibly loud that their calls have been recorded traveling over 4 miles through the air - they're essentially the foghorns of the bird world, and their voice is so powerful it can actually be felt as vibrations through your chest when you're close to them!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with trumpeter swans, but whooper swans have that distinctive yellow-and-black bill pattern (yellow extending past the nostrils), while trumpeter swans have all-black bills. Think "yellow whooper, black trumpeter" to remember the difference.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the "common swan" in Europe, whooper swans are anything but common in New England - with only 3 recorded observations ever, seeing one here would be a once-in-a-lifetime birding experience that should definitely be reported to eBird and local birding communities.
compareHints: Compared to the much more common mute swan, whooper swans lack the orange bill and prominent forehead knob, instead showing that diagnostic yellow-and-black bill pattern. Unlike trumpeter swans, which have all-black bills, the whooper's yellow bill is unmistakable. Whooper swans are also much more vocal than mute swans and hold their necks straighter than the curved-neck posture typical of mutes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Trumpeter Swans, which have straight black bills and are much larger, Mute Swans have that telltale orange bill with black markings.
Trumpeter Swans are larger and more vocal than Mute Swans, with completely black bills versus the Mute Swan's orange bill with black knob.
Tundra Swans are much smaller than Trumpeter Swans and have yellow spots on their bills, while Trumpeters have all-black bills and deeper, more bugle-like calls.

Unlike the common Mute Swan with its white plumage and orange bill, or the Trumpeter and Tundra Swans with their white bodies and black bills, the Black Swan is the only swan species with entirely black plumage.
Unlike our familiar Mute Swan with its all-white plumage and orange bill, the Black-necked Swan's dramatic two-toned coloring is unmistakable.
